The open issue is how far public marketing of the property (as opposed to the contract) may go before it becomes brokerage.

Code 1101.0045(a), as amended by SB 1577 (eff. 2024-01-01), lets a person acquire an option or contract interest and then sell or assign it without a license if the person (1) does not use it to engage in real estate brokerage and (2) discloses in writing the nature of the equitable interest to any seller or potential buyer. wholesaler_registration_required.note: No wholesaler registration exists in the statutes reviewed; the regime is disclosure-based. TREC's 2022 survey article says wholesalers need not be licensed if they disclose their interest to potential buyers and do not otherwise broker.

license_required_for_activity.note: Not required for repeated assignments if the written disclosures are made and the person does not engage in brokerage (for example acting for the seller or buyer, negotiating for others, or listing the property). The statute has no frequency threshold. Assigning or offering to assign without the disclosure is itself brokerage (1101.0045(b)), so a missed disclosure converts the activity into unlicensed practice.

disclosures_required.note: Two written disclosures are required by Prop. Code 5.0205 (moved from 5.086 and amended by SB 1577) and Occ. Code 1101.0045(a)(2). The statute sets the timing as before entering into a contract to sell the option or assign the interest; a licensed broker's 2026 article (secondary) reads the seller notice as due before the purchase agreement is signed, which is the conservative practice.

public_marketing_permitted.note: The statute contemplates offering to sell an option or assign a contract to potential buyers, and TREC describes wholesaling as marketing an option or equitable interest, so marketing the contract interest with the written disclosure is permitted. Advertising the property as if owned or listed (MLS listing, undisclosed yard signs) is described by a licensed Texas broker (secondary) as unlicensed brokerage. No TREC rule defining permissible wholesale advertising content was found.

direct_investor_outreach_permitted.note: Permitted as marketing of the principal's own contract interest, provided each potential buyer gets the written disclosure that only a contract interest is offered and the assignor lacks legal title before the assignment contract is signed.

assignment_restrictions.note: No statutory prohibition or seller-consent requirement was found. Prop. Code 5.0205 conditions assignment on the written buyer disclosure and owner notice. Whether the purchase contract itself is assignable is a contract question; a Texas firm (secondary) advises stating assignability expressly in a residential earnest money contract.

double_closing_permitted.note: No statute addresses double closings. A licensed Texas brokerage's 2026 article (secondary) says they are lawful but that many national title underwriters decline simultaneous closings. If the property is offered to the end buyer before the first closing, the principal is still offering an equitable interest, so treating the 1101.0045/5.0205 disclosures as applicable is the safe reading (inference for counsel).

seller_cancellation_right.note: Neither Occ. Code 1101.0045 nor Prop. Code 5.0205 gives the seller a cancellation right, and none was found in this research. Counsel should confirm that no other consumer statute applies to these contracts.

local_restrictions.note: No city or county wholesaling rules were found. A Houston broker's 2026 article (secondary) reports no Houston or Harris County-specific rules, but other cities were not checked.

out_of_state_entity_requirements.note: A foreign LLC transacting business in Texas must register with the Secretary of State under Business Organizations Code ch. 9 (Form 304, $750 fee) and keep a Texas registered agent and office (it cannot be its own agent; a mailbox service is not enough). Late filing fees apply once business has been transacted more than 90 days without registration. Franchise tax obligations with the Comptroller were not verified here.

draft.summary: Research dated 2026-10-22 (confidence: low). Not reviewed by counsel. Florida has no wholesaling-specific statute, disclosure rule, or registration; the question turns on the brokerage licensing law, Fla. Stat. ch. 475, which covers persons who, for another and for compensation, sell, buy, negotiate, or advertise real property interests, and makes a single act sufficient. Unlicensed brokerage is a third-degree felony and compensation agreements for unlicensed brokerage are unenforceable. The common position that a principal may assign its own contract but must not market the property rests on secondary sources; no Florida Real Estate Commission guidance or 2024-2026 wholesaling bill was found. Proposed classification A: No Florida statute or rule imposes wholesaling-specific registration, disclosure, notice, or cancellation conditions, and the license law reaches only acts done 'for another', which on its face excludes a principal assigning its own contract. That fits A. Confidence is low because no regulator guidance or case confirming the principal-assignment reading was found, the single-act rule and felony penalty raise the stakes, and secondary sources treat advertising the property itself as brokerage, which would push toward D for any public property marketing.

principal_assignment_without_license.note: The ch. 475 broker definition is limited to acts done for another for compensation (475.01(1)(a)); a principal assigning its own contract interest is commonly treated as outside it (secondary). No statute, rule, FREC/DBPR statement or case confirming this for repeated assignments was found. The 475.011 owner exemption covers persons dealing in property they own, which a contract holder may not be.

wholesaler_registration_required.note: No wholesaler-specific statute or registration was found; secondary sources state Florida has no wholesaling statute and regulates the activity only through ch. 475.

license_required_for_activity.note: A license is required where the person acts for another for compensation, including advertising or procuring buyers for another's property. 475.01(3) makes a single act sufficient, so there is no frequency threshold or repeat-activity safe harbor. Unlicensed practice is a third-degree felony (475.42) and compensation for unlicensed brokerage is unenforceable (475.41).

disclosures_required.note: No wholesaling-specific disclosure or notice requirement was found in Florida statutes or in the sources reviewed.

public_marketing_permitted.note: Secondary sources say an unlicensed principal may advertise its assignable contract interest, but publicly advertising the property itself (MLS, Zillow-type listings) is treated as brokerage. Not confirmed by FREC or DBPR guidance; counsel must decide what advertising content is safe.

direct_investor_outreach_permitted.note: Offering one's own contract interest to known investors is not on its face an act 'for another' under 475.01(1)(a), so it is likely outside the license requirement; supported only by statutory text and secondary sources.

assignment_restrictions.note: No Florida statute restricting, conditioning, or requiring consent for assignment of residential purchase contracts was found in this research.

double_closing_permitted.note: 475.011 exempts persons selling property they own, but the exemption is lost if an agent, employee, or contractor paid on a transactional basis conducts the sales. Reselling after taking title therefore appears exempt if Hālo's dispositions staff are not paid per transaction; marketing to the end buyer before the first closing raises the same questions as contract marketing.

seller_cancellation_right.note: No wholesaling-specific or general statutory seller cancellation right was identified; not researched beyond ch. 475.

local_restrictions.note: No city or county wholesaling rules were found; local rules were not specifically researched.

out_of_state_entity_requirements.note: Fla. Stat. 605.0902 requires a foreign LLC to apply for a certificate of authority to transact business (Form CR2E027) with a certificate of existence no more than 90 days old and a Florida registered agent with a Florida street address.

Foreign entity registration with the Secretary of State

W.S. 33-28-102 defines real estate activity as listed acts (including dealing in options and procuring prospects) performed by an individual for another and for compensation, and 33-28-104 treats a single such act for another as acting as a licensee. The 2026 amendments (SF0105) changed licensee disclosure rules but added nothing on wholesaling. principal_assignment_without_license.note: Real estate activity requires acting for another and for compensation (W.S. 33-28-102 'real estate activity'; 33-28-104), so a principal assigning its own contract appears outside licensing; no Commission guidance found.

wholesaler_registration_required.note: Title 33, chapter 28 contains no wholesaler registration; the 2026 amendments (SF0105) did not add one.

license_required_for_activity.note: A license is required for any single act of real estate activity for another, including procuring prospects and dealing in options for another. No frequency threshold found.

public_marketing_permitted.note: Advertising or holding out as engaged in the business of buying or selling real estate is listed real estate activity, though still framed by 'for another'; untested for principals.

direct_investor_outreach_permitted.note: Not addressed by any source found.

assignment_restrictions.note: No statutory consent, notice or prohibition on assignment was found.

double_closing_permitted.note: Buying and reselling for its own account is not an act for another, and W.S. 33-28-103(a)(i) exempts owners for property they own; counsel to confirm.

seller_cancellation_right.note: No statutory seller cancellation right for an ordinary wholesale purchase contract was found; foreclosure-rescue or equity-purchaser statutes (if any) were not verified.

local_restrictions.note: No city or county wholesaling rules were found in this research pass; not affirmatively ruled out.

out_of_state_entity_requirements.note: A foreign LLC applies to the Secretary of State for a certificate of authority (form cites W.S. 17-16-1533), names a Wyoming registered agent with a physical address, and pays a $150 fee.

sources.title: Wyoming Statutes Title 33 (Professions and Occupations), chapter 28
sources.summary: Defines real estate activity as listed acts by an individual for another and for compensation, exempts owners, and treats a single act for another as acting as a licensee.

counsel_questions: Does any Florida statute give a residential seller a right to cancel a purchase contract with an investor buyer, for example a home-solicitation or equity-purchaser rule?
If the Florida purchase contract is silent on assignment, does Florida law require the seller's consent to assign it?
